title: India's New Labour Codes Extend Minimum Wage to All Workers
excerpt: Four landmark codes effective November 2025 abolish 'scheduled employment' limits, covering 500 million-plus workers for the first time.
body:
India's Ministry of Labour and Employment made history on November 21, 2025, activating four sweeping Labour Codes that dismantle the colonial-era scaffolding governing how 500 million workers earn, work, and claim benefits. The reform, notified via the Official Gazette, collapses 29 existing labour statutes into a single, modern framework.

**What Changed on Minimum Wage:**
The headline shift is deceptively simple but enormously consequential. Under the old Minimum Wages Act, 1948, statutory wage protection applied only to workers in 'scheduled employments' — a list covering roughly 30% of the workforce. Earlier, the Minimum Wages Act applied only to scheduled employments, covering approximately 30% of workers. The new Code on Wages abolishes that list entirely. The concept of scheduled employment has been done away with under the Code on Wages, which is now universally applicable to all employees, irrespective of sector or category. Alongside this, a single statutory definition of 'wages' now applies across all four codes, and wages must form at least 50% of total remuneration, meaning allowances cannot be used excessively to reduce Provident Fund, bonus, gratuity, and other statutory payouts.

**Why It Matters Beyond the Factory Floor:**
Over the past decade, India expanded social-security coverage from about 19% of the workforce in 2015 to more than 64% in 2025. The new codes push further still. Gig workers and platform workers are now formally recognised, with provisions for aggregator contributions to a social security fund, and social security also expands to fixed-term, unorganised sector, and inter-state migrant workers. Gratuity eligibility drops from five years of service to one — a significant win for contract and fixed-term staff. Employers may experience a dual compliance environment where legacy state legislation continues to apply until superseded.

**What to Watch Next:**
The full impact will unfold only as state-level rules are finalised; until then, the transition remains incomplete, and employers must stay prepared for further adjustments.
